Journal of Management Studies, 22(4), 384–399] dimensions of power, the model reconceptualises legitimacy as a negotiated and relational process emerging through recursive interactions among regulators, standard-setters, and stakeholder groups. Extending Suchman’s legitimacy framework, it introduces relational legitimacy to capture perceived consensus regarding new accounting and reporting systems, within and across stakeholder groups. This concept becomes salient under conditions of contestation and political conflict. The model highlights meso-level actors’ role in mediating global standards and domestic contexts; and in managing tensions among pragmatic, moral, and cognitive legitimacy claims. Using several theoretical propositions and illustrative examples from financial and sustainability reporting, instrumental and symbolic power strategies are shown to be recursively intertwined, and their alignment can progressively engender relational and cognitive legitimacy of new national systems based on international standards.This paper challenges top-down accounts of standard-setting by theorising legitimacy and power as dynamically co-evolving, offering a foundation for future research on accounting and reporting regulation.
reason: Reconceptualises legitimacy as relational/negotiated and introduces a new type ('relational legitimacy') extending Suchman — meets 'defines or redefines' and 'proposes new types/dimensions'.

title: The Narrative Construction of Internal Organizational Legitimacy
abstract: Abstract Organizations torn by significant contradictions may struggle to maintain internal legitimacy. Taking a narrative perspective, and drawing on a case study of Walgreens, a Fortune 500 retail pharmacy, we develop a process model that shows how organizations with an entrenched conflict in their official narratives manage the resulting polyphony of members' personal narratives through the development of myths that sustain internal legitimacy by making the contradiction ‘liveable’. The model reveals how myths that represent contradictions as temporary and project a future in which they will be satisfactorily resolved help people to cope with inconsistencies in processes of organizing and support the status quo . Our theorizing suggests that internal legitimacy is constituted by the narratives that individuals author about the desirability, propriety, and appropriateness of their organization and its practices. From a narratological perspective, rather than existing on a continuum from high to low and being a resource that can be stockpiled, internal legitimacy may be theorized as a polyphony of distinctive narratives that while discursively dynamic is also generally durable.
reason: Theorizes internal legitimacy as a polyphony of narratives rather than a stockpiled resource on a continuum, explicitly revising the construct's nature and level (individual narratives within organization).

title: Oscillatory Legitimacy in Sustainability: Navigating Polarized Stakeholder Evaluations
abstract: ABSTRACT In contexts of heightened moral and institutional pluralism, corporate sustainability strategy is evaluated through divergent and often polarized stakeholder lenses. Under such conditions, the relationship between sustainability and business performance becomes a contested terrain of interpretation rather than a settled strategic fact. This article introduces the concept of oscillatory legitimacy to explain how organizations sustain credibility when legitimacy cannot be stabilized within a single evaluative frame. Oscillatory legitimacy conceptualizes legitimacy not as a reservoir of support, but as a dynamic process of movement across incompatible moral and pragmatic evaluations. Rather than reflecting deliberate strategic alternation, this movement is introduced by the structure of polarized stakeholder judgments, through which organizations are differently recognized as legitimate across audiences and over time. Drawing on legitimacy and stakeholder theory, the article develops a two‐dimensional framework centered on compatibility—the perceived strategic fit of sustainability—and interdependence—the perceived moral inseparability of sustainability from legitimate corporate purpose. Crossing these dimensions yields four ideal‐typical legitimacy configurations—integrative, instrumental, fragmented, and contested—and reveals patterned trajectories through which organizations navigate shifting expectations. Reframing legitimacy as oscillatory, the framework advances sustainability strategy research and demonstrates how credibility is sustained through movement rather than alignment in a polarized environment, with important implications for the depth and durability of sustainability outcomes.
reason: Introduces and theorizes a new concept—'oscillatory legitimacy'—redefining legitimacy as dynamic process and proposing dimensions/configurations, i.e., conceptual work on the construct.

title: A lot to chew on: expanding the frame of nordic nutrition recommendations 2023 to embrace health, transparency and environmental sustainability
abstract: Abstract How do expert committees sustain credibility while radically expanding their institutional scope? This question animates contemporary food governance, as dietary guidelines, historically focused on nutritional adequacy, increasingly incorporate environmental sustainability and demands for democratic participation. Yet scholarship has largely neglected the ongoing legitimacy work, the strategic framing, methodological commitments, and communication practices through which expert bodies navigate such frame expansion. This study takes the Nordic Nutrition Recommendations 2023 (NNR2023) as a critical case, analysing how experts reconciled scientific authority with environmental values and public participation. Drawing on in-depth expert interviews and an extensive documentary corpus, and bringing framing theory into conversation with a further developed, three-dimensional account of legitimacy, we distinguish epistemic, procedural, and cultural registers, the last of which we elaborate beyond its conventional treatment to foreground civic epistemologies and Nordic food cultures. Our findings show that these dimensions constantly pull against one another: methodological hardening strengthened epistemic authority yet narrowed participation; radical transparency enhanced fairness yet exposed disagreements; cultural accommodation honoured national foodways yet strained universalist claims. Rather than resolving these tensions, experts managed them through what we term “performed legitimacy,” an ongoing, audience-relational accomplishment that may suggest the contours of a more reflexive expert governance for an era of integrative food policy.
reason: Develops a three-dimensional account of legitimacy (epistemic, procedural, cultural) and proposes 'performed legitimacy' as an audience-relational concept, thus revising dimensions of the construct.

title: “Distributive fiscal justice” as a new dimension of corporate legitimacy in climate governance: a conceptual insight and foresight
venue: International Journal of Ethics and Systems
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this conceptual paper is to understand how corporate tax transparency shapes social equity in climate governance. Design/methodology/approach Through a qualitative, theory-building design, grounded in a systematic literature review, this study brings together environmental justice theory, legitimacy theory, institutional theory and political economy to develop an integrative conceptual framework that challenges existing assumptions, using a critical theorist standpoint. Findings The synthesis outcomes indicate that fiscal legitimacy is constituted across three interdependent dimensions – procedural, cognitive and distributive – and that prevailing environmental, social and governance (ESG) frameworks capture only the first. The study provides a normative standard for evaluating whether corporate tax practices contribute equitably to public revenues in climate-vulnerable jurisdictions. It theorises a structural fiscal-climatic injustice cycle through which corporate tax avoidance may constrain domestic adaptation finance in Global South countries, a synthesis outcome advanced as theoretically plausible rather than as an established causal claim. Research limitations/implications This study is conceptual and does not include primary empirical data, which limits the strength of causal claims. Future research should apply quantitative methodologies to test the fiscal-climatic injustice cycle and assess whether mandatory country-by-country reporting regimes demonstrably improve adaptation finance adequacy. Case study research in high-vulnerability, low-income country contexts – particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa and Small Island Developing States – is essential to operationalise distributive fiscal justice with country-specific baselines. The effective-tax-rate gap, revenue-profit alignment ratio and adaptation finance contribution gap indicators warrant testing in specific national and sectoral settings, particularly climate-vulnerable jurisdictions. Practical implications For companies, this study recommends conducting fiscal legitimacy audits and voluntarily publishing total tax contribution reports alongside sustainability disclosures. Board-level tax governance mechanisms should be established, with fiscal coherence indicators that explicitly link tax disclosures to climate policy outcomes. For ESG rating agencies and standard setters, the study provides a blueprint for integrating a distributive fiscal justice pillar into assessment architectures. For governments in developing countries, corporate fiscal responsibility should be recognised as a climate finance issue. United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change negotiations should incorporate corporate tax transparency provisions into climate finance mechanisms. Social implications The study highlights structural harms that disproportionately affect communities in the Global South. It identifies this harm as a manifestation of distributive injustice and incorporates it into ESG governance discourse, thereby generating normative pressure for systemic reform. Repositioning corporate fiscal conduct as a social equity issue has the potential to shift the terms of climate finance advocacy, empowering affected communities and their governments to make legitimate claims about the fiscal contributions of companies operating within their borders. Originality/value The study proposes a construct dubbed “distributive fiscal justice”, a new sub-dimension of fiscal legitimacy that captures the equity implications of corporate tax behaviour and links individual company behaviour to collective climate vulnerability. It reveals areas where the prevailing ESG and corporate social responsibility disclosure frameworks fall short of equity demands. It positions tax transparency as a non-negotiable foundation for equitable climate governance. It offers five theoretical propositions that inform the empirical agenda and policy reform.
reason: Conceptual paper that proposes a new dimension/sub-dimension of corporate legitimacy ('distributive fiscal justice' within fiscal legitimacy), i.e., revises types/dimensions of the construct.

title: Legitimacy Foundations
abstract: Abstract This chapter examines the burgeoning scholarship on legitimacy and briefly summarises the intellectual trajectory of this important concept. It discusses current conversations in legitimacy research and suggests future research directions that are necessary not only to advance scholarship on organisational legitimacy but also to inform the broader field of organisational social evaluations. It recommends that scholars build richer connections between levels of analysis both theoretically and empirically, expanding on the multilevel perspective on legitimacy that has developed rich linkages between societal and individual levels. Recognising that one of the most important research frontiers in the next decade is empirical in nature, the chapter also develop methodological recommendations, specifically for the development of instruments to measure individual-level legitimacy, the aggregation of individual-level measures into collective-level legitimacy, and the behavioural implications of legitimacy judgements.
reason: Reviews and takes stock of the legitimacy concept, its intellectual trajectory, and levels of analysis — meets 'reviews, takes stock of, or critiques the concept itself'.

title: Double Legitimacy in Member‐Driven Organizations: The Complementarity of Formal and Relational Governance in SACCO Performance
abstract: ABSTRACT Governance research has traditionally emphasized either formal structures of accountability or relational mechanisms of trust, often treating them as substitutes. This study advances a different view by conceptualizing governance as a system of double legitimacy: formal mechanisms confer external credibility, while relational mechanisms generate internal moral authority. Drawing on survey data from 458 Savings and Credit Cooperative Societies (SACCOs) in Kenya, this study examines how these dimensions interact to shape organizational performance. Hierarchical linear and polynomial regression analyses show that performance is highest when structural accountability and relational trust coexist. Formal governance—through audits, elections, and by‐law enforcement—safeguards solidarity from opportunism, while relational governance—through fairness, conflict resolution, and trust—renders rules legitimate in the eyes of members. The results confirm that neither dimension is sufficient on its own: organizations relying exclusively on formal rules risk disengagement, while those depending solely on trust lack external legitimacy. The study makes four contributions. First, it extends institutional theory by showing how hybrid governance forms are sustained through relational practices as well as structural adoption. Second, it advances relational governance research by theorizing relational governance as an intra‐organizational dynamic. Third, it develops legitimacy theory through the construct of double legitimacy, highlighting the recursive interaction of compliance and trust. Finally, it challenges conventional views of authority boundaries by showing that blurred roles can recycle legitimacy across domains, sustaining governance under weak institutional enforcement. Beyond SACCOs, these insights apply to schools, NGOs, churches, and other member‐driven organizations where authority depends on both rules and relationships.
reason: Proposes a 'double legitimacy' construct distinguishing formal/external and relational/internal dimensions, thus proposing dimensions/components of legitimacy rather than merely using it as a variable.

title: Legitimacy in contested issue fields: How type‐based validity cues, cue congruence, and personal values shape propriety
abstract: Abstract Contested business practices are often difficult to evaluate because they send multiple, often conflicting signals about their appropriateness. Some cues may suggest that a practice is useful, legal, or widely accepted, whereas others may suggest that it is risky, harmful, or socially opposed. Existing legitimacy research has typically examined validity cues through source‐based classifications, namely, authorization and endorsement, and has more often considered such cues in isolation than as part of wider evaluative arrangements. This study shifts the analysis of validity cues from source‐based to type‐based classifications by focusing on cues corresponding to four major legitimacy types: normative, pragmatic, regulatory, and cognitive. It argues that when evaluators confront multiple validity cues simultaneously, propriety judgments depend not only on the presence of those cues but also on their relative weight, on whether they are consistent or contradictory, and on whether they align with evaluators' personal values. These dynamics are examined in the context of fracking through four heterogeneous cues: public opinion, economic impact, regulatory setting, and venture longevity. Using conjoint analysis in a novel application to microlevel legitimacy research, the study analyzes 3,952 evaluations by 247 participants in France and Spain. Findings show that evaluators assign different weights to type‐based validity cues, with economic impact exerting the strongest influence, followed by public opinion and regulatory setting. We introduce cue congruence to legitimacy theory, defined as the extent to which multiple validity cues convey aligned evaluative signals about the legitimacy of a subject, and show that positively congruent combinations generate higher propriety judgments, negatively congruent ones generate lower judgments, and incongruent combinations generate more intermediate ones. Moreover, we introduce cue‐value congruence, that is, whether cue combinations align with evaluators' personal values, and show that evaluators high in environmentalism are less influenced by cues that conflict with their values. The study therefore explains how legitimacy judgments emerge from multiple cues considered jointly and shows that conflicting cues generate intermediate propriety beliefs, consistent with a gray area between clear legitimacy and clear illegitimacy at the microlevel.
reason: Engages the construct itself: reclassifies validity cues from source-based to type-based, introduces new concepts (cue congruence, cue-value congruence), and works at the microlevel propriety/validity distinction—conceptual development and releveling.

title: Keeping Up With the Times? Rethinking Social Evaluations Research Under Contemporary Technological and Sociopolitical Forces
abstract: Abstract The context within which social evaluations form has been fundamentally altered by contemporary forces, such as digital technologies, polarization, activism, politicization of business, and geopolitical tensions. While research on social evaluations has generated rich insights into the formation and development of constructs, such as legitimacy, status, reputation, stigma, trust, and celebrity, much of this work has been developed under the assumptions of relative stability, coherent audiences, and well‐defined intermediary roles. These assumptions are increasingly challenged in this changing context, requiring us to rethink the formation and management of social evaluations. The articles in this special issue focus on these changes. Building on these contributions, this introductory article develops a research agenda across seven interconnected areas: the stability and fragility of social evaluations, audience fragmentation and convergence, the reshaping of the intermediary landscape, construct interrelationships, range and extension of constructs, the measurement of social evaluations, and their underlying foundations. We discuss how these transformations affect not only organizations and evaluative processes, but also the societal impact of social evaluations. Overall, this editorial provides a framework to guide future research in a field undergoing profound transition.
reason: Critiques and takes stock of social evaluation constructs including legitimacy, addressing construct interrelationships/boundaries with status, reputation, trust, and foundations/measurement — conceptual work on the construct.

title: Performing legitimacy: philanthropic foundations and the embeddedness of privatisation in Chilean public schools
venue: Discourse Studies in the Cultural Politics of Education
abstract: Philanthropic organisations have become increasingly influential in education systems, yet little is known about how their legitimacy is produced within schools. This article shifts attention from philanthropy’s macro-level influence on education policy to the school-level dynamics through which philanthropic actors become legitimate in Chilean public schools. Drawing on organisational legitimacy theory and its performative and discursive extensions, the study analyses two case studies of foundations working in public schools, based on interviews, observations, and document analysis. Findings identify three interconnected forms of legitimacy underpinning school actors’ positive evaluations of philanthropy: pragmatic legitimacy, linked to foundations’ capacity to compensate for state shortcomings; technical legitimacy, built through expertise, evidence, and evaluation; and emotional legitimacy, grounded in affective relations of care and recognition. Through these findings, the article shows how philanthropic legitimacy is performatively enacted through everyday practices, expert authority, and affective ties, sustaining the embedded presence of private actors in public education.
reason: Proposes/revises types of legitimacy (pragmatic, technical, emotional) and engages performative/discursive conceptualization, meeting 'proposes or revises its types, dimensions or components'.

title: Legitimacy and Employment Relations Research: A Review and Research Agenda
venue: Industrial Relations A Journal of Economy and Society
abstract: ABSTRACT This article provides a comprehensive review of existing research and develops an agenda for analyzing legitimacy in employment relations. It argues that legitimacy should be understood as a dynamic and contested process through which actors, institutions and policy ideas are legitimated, delegitimated and reworked. The article examines the legitimacy of employment relations ideas, the relationship between legitimacy, power and politics, the legitimacy of employment relations actors and of employment relations as a field of study. It concludes by locating the articles in this special issue within this broad agenda and draws out key insights for legitimacy research in employment relations.
reason: Reviews and critiques the concept of legitimacy itself, arguing it should be understood as a dynamic contested process (redefinition/reviewing the concept).

title: Legitimacy
abstract: Abstract This chapter examines legitimacy as the judgement employees make about whether their organization’s stated purpose aligns with their own values (propriety) and whether colleagues genuinely endorse it (validity). It argues that legitimacy is not a static attribute that leadership can project through communication but a dynamic assessment continuously shaped by observed behaviour at the team level. The chapter demonstrates that introducing a purpose yields a baseline performance increase of approximately 10%. However, team composition decisively moderates this effect: When an explicit prosocial purpose is matched with a high-prosociality team, performance gains reach 34%, whereas imposing the same purpose on a low-prosociality team degrades performance by 13% below the no-purpose baseline. The chapter illustrates these dynamics through cases, including BrewDog, whose prosocial workforce became its most damaging critics when leadership behaviour contradicted stated values, and Wells Fargo, where a corrupt de facto purpose overrode the official one. The identified blocker is mismatch between purpose content and team motivational composition. The chapter concludes with practical guidance on assessing team prosocial orientation and differentiating leadership strategies accordingly.
reason: Chapter conceptualizes legitimacy via propriety/validity, relevels it to individual/team judgement and argues it is dynamic rather than a static attribute — meets 'defines/redefines' and 'level of analysis' criteria.

title: Legitimacy Dynamics
abstract: Abstract Legitimacy is central to organisational institutionalism, shaping how organisations conform to societal norms while navigating evolving institutional landscapes. This chapter examines legitimacy dynamics across four conversations: organisational hybridity, optimal distinctiveness, institutional entrepreneurship, and institutional trust. The first explores hybrid organisations, particularly social enterprises, balancing competing logics and legitimacy pressures. The second addresses optimal distinctiveness, where organisations navigate the tension between conformity and differentiation to maintain competitive advantage. The third focuses on institutional entrepreneurship, highlighting how organisations shape or resist shifting legitimacy criteria at the field level. The fourth considers institutional trust, maintenance, and restoration, emphasising the need for studies of legitimacy dynamics that account for grand societal challenges like inequality, climate change, and the erosion of democratic values. By integrating these themes, the chapter underscores the dynamic, contested nature of legitimacy. It calls for further exploration of how organisations adapt to shifting societal expectations, negotiate legitimacy in polarised fields, and sustain institutional resilience.
reason: Review/stock-taking chapter that critiques and theorizes the legitimacy concept itself (its dynamic, contested nature) across conversations, including boundary with institutional trust.

title: Legitimacy in Practice
abstract: Abstract This chapter provides a practitioner’s view on the role of legitimacy in organisational success, with reference to both the organisation and its leadership. It also outlines the role of legitimacy in obtaining and retaining resources such as talent and investment. The chapter describes legitimacy as a gateway to other social evaluations such as trust and reputation and as a social licence to operate. This chapter provides practical examples of the various types of legitimacy achieved by organisations and illustrates them with seven real-world examples. These are drawn from the author’s first-hand experience from companies including: Clear Channel, MSQ Partners, Shakespeare’s Globe, Uber, and YouGov. It suggests that the notion of legitimacy is rarely discussed in boardrooms, unlike the more familiar social evaluations. But legitimacy is often sought as part of a path to other organisational goals. The chapter illustrates the various routes to achieving organisational legitimacy. These include having it conferred by, for example: a stock market listing; awarded by a regulatory body; by qualifying to be accepted into a bidding process; by association with highly regarded professional advisers; by demonstration of results; by acclaim from the public or peers; and by assertion when legitimacy is claimed and not disputed. The chapter calls for academic research into robust methods to assess legitimacy and describes an organisation status in this context.
reason: Chapter engages the construct itself: positions legitimacy relative to neighboring social evaluations (trust, reputation, status) and delineates types/routes to legitimacy, meeting the boundary-setting and typology criteria.
